lesson.title: Measuring Resistance: Only When the Power Is Off
lesson.summary: A multimeter measures resistance by pushing its own small known signal through the component and reading the response, which only works correctly, and only works safely, on a circuit that has no power of its own applied.
lesson.body:
When you measure voltage or current, you are reading something the circuit itself is producing, a source elsewhere is doing the work and the meter is just observing. Measuring resistance works the opposite way: the multimeter itself supplies a small, known test current (or voltage) through its probes, measures the resulting voltage (or current), and calculates resistance internally using Ohm's law before displaying the result. Because the meter is providing its own tiny internal source for this measurement, the circuit or component under test must not have any of its own power applied.

If you try to measure a resistor's value while it is still connected in a circuit that has its own battery or power supply attached and switched on, that external voltage combines with the meter's own internal test signal in ways the meter was never designed to handle. At best you get a meaningless or wildly inaccurate reading; at worst, especially with meters whose internal resistance sensing circuitry can be overloaded by an unexpected external voltage, you can damage the meter itself. The rule is simple and worth internalizing: before switching a multimeter to its resistance function, power the circuit down completely.

As a concrete example, imagine a resistor wired into a circuit with a 9 volt battery. If you leave the battery connected and probe across the resistor with the meter set to measure ohms, the reading will be unreliable or the meter may show an overload indication. Disconnect the battery first, or better yet, lift one leg of the resistor out of the circuit entirely, then probe across it, and the meter will show its actual resistance accurately. That second refinement, lifting one leg free of the rest of the circuit, matters because if the resistor still has other components wired in parallel with it, even with the power off, the meter will measure the combined resistance of all those parallel paths together rather than the resistor alone, giving a lower reading than the resistor's true value.
